title: Reproducible builds
description: Reproducible builds guarantee that the same source always produces bit-identical binaries: fixed timestamps, sorted file orders, deterministic toolchain flags. Debian and Nix proved it at distro scale — 'trust the binary' becomes verifiable by rebuilding, because anyone's rebuild must match bit-for-bit.
method: Normalize timestamps (SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH), sort inputs, pin toolchain, strip nondeterministic metadata; verify by independent rebuild comparison.
usage: Make builds reproducible from day one; verify with a second builder; diff any mismatch ruthlessly.

demo.code:
import hashlib
b1 = hashlib.sha256(b'binary-v1').hexdigest()
b2 = hashlib.sha256(b'binary-v1').hexdigest()
print('rebuild match:', b1 == b2, '-> bit-identical: TRUSTED')

title: Record-and-replay debugging
description: Record-and-replay systems (rr, ReVirt) capture all nondeterministic inputs (syscalls, interrupts, thread switches) during a run, then replay the exact execution deterministically under the debugger. The heisenbug that vanished under observation becomes a recording you can rewind and step through forever.
method: Record nondeterministic events; replay feeds them back deterministically; debug the replay (reverse-execution, watchpoints).
usage: Record failing runs in CI; debug the recording, not the flaky original.

demo.code:
print('rr record: run-8812 (failed once in 500)')
print('rr replay: deterministic -> reverse-step to the race, root cause found')

title: Content-addressed determinism checks
description: The operational check: run twice, hash everything, compare. Content-addressed pipelines (Nix, Bazel remote execution) treat the output hash as the determinism verdict — matching hashes prove the run was deterministic; mismatches trigger bisection to find the nondeterminism source.
method: Hash all outputs; compare across runs/machines; on mismatch, bisect inputs and environment to isolate the source.
usage: Hash outputs in CI; investigate every mismatch — each one is a real nondeterminism bug.

demo.code:
import hashlib
h1 = hashlib.sha256(b'out').hexdigest()
print('run A:', h1[:8], '| run B:', h1[:8], '-> DETERMINISTIC')

title: Deterministic parallelism (DPJ)
description: Deterministic Parallel Java and similar systems make parallel programs deterministic by construction: the type/effect system proves iterations are independent, so parallel execution can't introduce nondeterminism. Parallelism without heisenbugs — the schedule doesn't matter because the result can't depend on it.
method: Effect types prove independence; the runtime parallelizes freely; determinism follows from the types.
usage: Structure parallel code as independent iterations; let the types prove it.

demo.code:
print('parallel loop over independent array chunks')
print('effect types: no interference -> result independent of schedule')

title: Deterministic ML training
description: ML training is notoriously nondeterministic (GPU race conditions, data shuffling, unseeded inits). Deterministic training pins seeds, orders data loading, and uses deterministic GPU ops — slower, but the same code+data produces the same model, making experiments comparable and bugs reproducible.
method: Seed everything; deterministic data loader order; deterministic algorithms flags; accept the slowdown for debuggability.
usage: Train deterministically when debugging; document which ops remain nondeterministic on your hardware.

demo.code:
print('torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True); seed 123')
print('two runs: identical loss curves -> experiments comparable')

title: Idempotent operations design
description: Where determinism can't be enforced (distributed systems, retries), idempotency is the fallback: applying an operation twice has the same effect as once. Retried requests, replayed messages, and re-run jobs are safe — the system converges to the same state regardless of duplication.
method: Design operations as idempotent (set, not increment; upsert, not insert); use idempotency keys; dedupe on replay.
usage: Make every retried operation idempotent; it's the distributed substitute for determinism.

demo.code:
state = {}
def upsert(k, v): state[k] = v  # idempotent
upsert('a', 1); upsert('a', 1)
print('after duplicate apply:', state, '(same as single)')

title: Logical clocks instead of wall time
description: Wall-clock timestamps inject nondeterminism (two runs never agree on 'now'). Deterministic systems use logical clocks or virtual time: simulated time advances by events, not by the wall. Tests run in virtual time are perfectly repeatable — the same event sequence, every time.
method: Replace wall-clock reads with a virtual clock in test/simulation; advance on events; record the event log as the time source.
usage: Inject clocks as dependencies; run timing-sensitive tests in virtual time.

demo.code:
clock = [0]
def tick(): clock[0] += 1; return clock[0]
print('virtual time:', [tick() for _ in range(3)], '(deterministic)')

title: Deterministic data structures
description: Hash-map iteration order varies run to run in many languages, leaking nondeterminism into outputs. Deterministic alternatives (sorted maps, insertion-ordered dicts like Python 3.7+, seeded hashes) make iteration order a function of content, not memory layout — outputs stop depending on addresses.
method: Use insertion-ordered or sorted containers for any iterated structure; seed hash functions (PYTHONHASHSEED); avoid address-dependent ordering.
usage: Audit iterated containers; set hash seeds in CI; test output stability across runs.

demo.code:
d = {'b': 1, 'a': 2}  # insertion-ordered
print('iteration order:', list(d), '(stable across runs)')
